title: What the homepage has to prove for a two-sided marketplace
metaTitle: What a marketplace homepage must prove
excerpt: Show one real match and a way to join the side you need first. Two equal buttons, with no example behind them, ask a cautious visitor to guess.
alt: An open notebook with the word Notes underlined, a fountain pen, and glasses on a wooden desk, for a homepage that has to record one marketplace match.
caption: A notebook open to the side of the market that has to arrive first. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Which side should a marketplace homepage speak to first?
faqs.answer: Speak first to the side that must arrive before the other side will trust the market. That is often the supply side, though it depends on the category. The first screen should show a match that side recognizes and a join path written in their words. The other side still needs a door, further down the page or on its own landing page.

faqs.question: What if the marketplace has no completed match to show yet?
faqs.answer: Use a clearly labeled sample built from the offer you will actually run, or publish the terms of the first match you are prepared to make. Name the city, the category, the fee, and what you will do by hand while the other side is thin. An invented customer with a fake saving trains the careful visitor to leave.

faqs.question: Should both sides get an equal button in the hero?
faqs.answer: Equal buttons look fair and refuse the seeding problem. Give the scarce side the primary action, with a label that says what they are joining. Offer the other side a quiet link to their own path. If a partner requires both controls on the first screen, keep the visual hierarchy pointed at the side you need first.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A two-sided marketplace homepage has one job for the side that has to show up first. It shows a concrete example of a match, then a way to join that side. Two equal buttons and no story ask a cautious person to guess what you want.

The other side can wait a screen. The side you need first cannot. Write the page in that order: one match, the join path, then the explanation. Everything else supports that sequence.

## Name the side that has to arrive first

A marketplace is two promises. One is supply. The other is demand. They are not equal on the day you launch. One of them is the reason the other will bother to come. A freight board needs carriers before a shipper will trust a listing. A care platform needs vetted workers before a family will book. A local services market needs enough pros in a city before a homeowner will post a job.

Write that side down in one sentence before anyone draws the homepage. "We need coaches in the city before athletes will pay." "We need hosts with real kitchens before diners will search." If the sentence is still vague, the page will speak to everyone and convince no one.

The sentence also names the proof. The match you show has to be a match that side recognizes. A coach needs a booked session with a sport, a time, and a fee. A host needs a dinner that filled. A carrier needs a lane, a date, and a rate. A diagram of "buyers and sellers" describes the company to itself. It does not show a market.

Keep the sentence where the team will see it: in the brief, at the top of the copy doc, and in the Figma frame for the first screen. When someone asks for a second hero button, read the sentence aloud. If the button does not help that side join, it waits.

## Show one match before you explain the model

The first screen is a single example. One match, with the particulars that make it believable. A category grid can come later. A manifesto can go.

Name the two parties in plain words. Name what moved between them. Name the outcome in the unit that side already uses: a booking, a filled shift, a paid invoice, a completed job. If you have a real match you are allowed to show, use it. If you are pre-launch, use a clearly labeled sample built from the offer you will actually run, and say it is a sample. An invented "Sarah in Brooklyn saved $400" is worse than a plain example. The cold side is already skeptical, and founders get caught.

Place the join path on that same screen. The label should say what they are joining. "List your kitchen." "Apply as a carrier." "Join as a coach." "Get started" is a label for a team that has not chosen a side.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on page time is the right pressure. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and a page has to communicate its value within about 10 seconds if you want them to stay long enough to read. On this homepage, that value is the match. The example has to be readable at a glance: who, what, and the control that lets the first side step in.

Put the match in the visitor's language, including the number they use to judge it. A coach cares that the session paid $80 and lasted an hour. A carrier cares that the lane was 400 miles and the rate was posted before the truck rolled. Leave the internal name of the feature off the screen. "Match card v3" is a file name. "Tuesday, 6pm, one table left" is a market.

## Why two equal buttons fail

Two buttons feel fair. "I'm a host" and "I'm a guest." "For brands" and "For creators." The symmetry looks like a product diagram. It also refuses to choose.

The side you need first does not experience the market as a balanced drawing. They experience a risk. Will I be the only one here? Will I build a profile and then hear nothing? A pair of equal buttons announces that you have not decided who you are asking. The visitor who is already unsure picks neither.

There is a second failure inside the symmetry. Each button tends to open a page written for both, or a signup that asks which side you are after the click. You have moved the decision into a form. Forms are where unsure people quit.

Give the first side the primary action. Give the other side a text link. "Looking to book? Browse open kitchens." That link can be quiet. It should not compete in weight, color, or placement with the join path. Fairness on the screen is not fairness in the market. The market gets fairer when the scarce side shows up.

If a partner or a launch plan requires both actions on the first screen, keep both, and still make the hierarchy obvious. A filled button and a quiet link can share a screen. Same destination is not the same emphasis.

## Write the rest of the page in that order

After the match and the join path, answer the three questions that side asks next.

What do I have to do? Three steps, in their words. Create a profile, set availability, get booked. Or: post a lane, name a rate, accept a carrier. Steps that describe your software ("onboard into the ecosystem") belong in a pitch deck, if they belong anywhere.

What happens while the other side is thin? Say the truth. If you are seeding one city, name the city, and say what you do while density is low. "We introduce you to the first ten clients" is a concrete promise if you will actually do it. "Join a thriving community" is a wish. If the founder is still matching people by hand, say that. Operators respect a person who is still in the middle of the market.

What does it cost to join? The full pricing page can live one click away. The shape of the price cannot. Free to list, fee on a completed booking. A subscription for the pro, no fee for the customer. A commission taken from the side that pays. Hide the shape and the careful visitor assumes the worst, or assumes you have not decided.

Only then add the second side's path, a short note on trust, and another proof module. Trust, here, means the specific mechanism: reviews after a completed job, a license check, insurance, payout timing. Name the one you actually run. A padlock icon is not a mechanism.

Google's people-first content guidance is a useful edit on this sequence. A homepage should leave a visitor able to act, and it should come from experience with the market. If a block could sit on any marketplace in any category, cut it or replace it with a particular from yours.

## Give the other side a door that is not the front door

Ignoring the second side creates a different failure. They will arrive from ads, from a shared link, and from invitations the first side sends. They need a door. They do not need the front door.

Put their path where a motivated visitor can find it: a navigation item in their language, a short section below the first screen, and a landing page you can send in a campaign. That page can lead with their job. The homepage should not.

Watch the words. The two sides often name the product differently. A family books "care." A worker picks up "shifts." If the homepage uses only the family's words, workers do not see themselves. The hero uses the first side's words. The secondary path uses the other side's words. Do not average them into a third vocabulary that nobody says out loud.

If both sides are truly scarce, you still pick a primary for the homepage and send the other to a dedicated page. Two scarce sides are an operations problem. The homepage cannot solve it by speaking in stereo.

## Proof you can stand behind

The second match on the page should be as specific as the first. Three lines are enough: who was on each side, what the constraint was, what completed. A count is allowed when it is true. If you have twelve completed matches, "twelve" is a stronger line than a rounded "dozens," and it is much stronger than a number you hope to reach by the end of the quarter.

Skip the logo wall unless those logos are sides of the market a visitor would recognize as peers. A row of tools you use, or accelerators that once emailed you, does not prove a match. It proves that the team has been in rooms.

If you cannot show a completed match yet, show the terms of the first one you are prepared to run. City, category, fee, and what you will do personally until the other side arrives. That is still a concrete offer. It is honest about the stage.

Keep proof close to the join path. A beautiful story at the bottom of a long page arrives after the decision to leave. The first screen carries one match. The next screen can carry a second, with the join path repeated. Repetition of the action is useful. Repetition of the company story is not.

## Check the first screen in ten seconds

Read the first screen on a phone, out loud. You should be able to say who the match is between, what was exchanged, and how the first side joins. If you have to scroll to learn any of those three, the screen is still a company introduction.

Then hand the phone to someone who fits the first side and is not on your team. Ask what they think you want them to do. If they say "sign up" but cannot say as what, the label is wrong. If they describe your mission and not a match, the example is too weak or too far down.

Ask what they would need to have ready. A license, a kitchen inspection, a bank account, a portfolio, a city. If the answer is on the page, the next click will not feel like a trap. If the answer is a surprise on the next screen, you will lose the careful people, who are the ones you want.

Run the same check after every addition. New sections accumulate because each one pleased someone in a meeting. The ten-second read is how you notice that the match has been pushed below a slogan, a metric, and a logo row.

Once a visitor believes a match is possible, they judge whether joining is worth the fee. That next decision is the [pricing page for a two-sided marketplace](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-two-sided-marketplace).
